DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection

**Verdict:** The pilot design is good and most of the arithmetic is correct, but three findings change the conclusions:
- the flats data contradicts the case for a uniform service;
- the tonnage projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot data;
- Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage.

Once these are corrected, the net cost very likely exceeds the £520,000 provisional allocation. The recommendation that the service is "fully funded" doesn't hold as written.

## 1. Participation was not similar across housing types
Table 1 shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**. Flats participate at less than a third of the rate of houses. Section 2, the recommendation and the cover note all say the opposite.

This is the most important finding in the pilot, and it points the other way from the study's conclusion. Low participation in flats is common. It usually needs a different approach, such as communal bins, bin-store placement and targeted engagement with managing agents. The study should recommend that tailored approach rather than rule it out. Flats make up about 20% of the district, roughly 10,400 households.

## 2. The projection uses 64%, not the pilot's 57%
Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but the pilot's overall rate is **57%**, and 64% doesn't appear anywhere in the data. The pilot's 20% share of flats matches the district's, so the pilot rates can be applied directly by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That's about **420 tonnes (13%) less** than the 3,290 projected.

Two further points:
- Participation in new schemes often falls after the launch period, and January to June doesn't capture any seasonal variation. A downside case would be prudent.
- The table measures "average weekly set-out," which is not the same as participation. Use one term consistently.

## 3. Brookfield's capacity is 1,800 tonnes, not the full tonnage
Section 4 states that Brookfield can take **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. Projected tonnage is 2,870 on corrected figures, or 3,290 on the study's own figures. That leaves **about 1,070–1,490 tonnes a year** with nowhere local to go. Yet the saving of £243,000 assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38. The cover note's statement that "treatment is local" therefore applies to only about 60% of the tonnage.

The remainder would need to go to the plant 46 miles away. That involves a gate fee the study doesn't state, plus much longer haulage: more vehicle time, and possibly a transfer arrangement. The study needs a quote and a costed haulage plan for the second plant, or another solution.

## 4. Revised funding position
The cost lines check out arithmetically:
- £990,000 of vehicles over 7 years is £141,400 a year.
- 12 operatives at £34,000 each is £408,000.
- The total is £733,400.
- The net cost of £490,400 is correct on the study's own inputs.

Correcting the inputs changes the result:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs. £520,000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| As written (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 under |
| Corrected tonnage, all at Brookfield (not possible) | £212,400 | £521,000 | £1,000 over |
| Corrected tonnage, 1,800 t at Brookfield, rest saving nothing | £133,200 | £600,200 | £80,200 over |

The real figure falls between the last two rows, depending on what the second plant costs. In every corrected case the service is **not** fully covered by the allocation.

Note that the study's margin was thin even before these corrections, at £30,000 on a provisional figure.

## 5. Costs missing from Table 2
The cover note says every cost line is shown, but several are absent:
- **Haulage and gate fees for tonnage above Brookfield's capacity** (see section 3).
- **Cover for absence and annual leave.** Six crews with no relief staff can't run a weekly service.
- **Supervision, management and the dedicated phone line** described in Section 6.
- **Recruitment and training costs.**
- **Capital funding.** The £990,000 vehicle purchase is needed upfront in December 2026, but the study shows only annual depreciation and doesn't say where the cash comes from. It also doesn't say whether the new-burdens allocation includes capital funding or covers revenue only.
- It isn't clear whether the £34,000 per operative includes on-costs such as employer pension and National Insurance.

## 6. Smaller points
- **Satisfaction figure.** Section 2 reports 81% of *surveyed* pilot households, but doesn't say who was surveyed or the response rate. If the survey reached mostly participating households, the figure overstates satisfaction.
- **Timetable.** Ordering vehicles in December for March delivery leaves no slack. Crews would train in March, caddies would go to 52,000 households in March, and collections would start on 5 April. A one-month vehicle delay pushes the start back. The study should include a contingency, such as hired vehicles.
- **Statutory deadline.** For most English councils, the deadline for weekly food waste collections was 31 March 2026. If Thornbury has a transitional arrangement allowing a later start, say so. If it doesn't, Cabinet should know the service is already late.
- **Liners after three months.** It isn't clear whether ongoing liner supply is included in the £88,000.

## 7. What holds up
- The pilot design: a reasonable sample, a mixed set of wards, and weekly data split by housing type.
- The Table 1 arithmetic. The per-household figures are internally consistent: the weighted average of 1.86 kg rounds to 1.9.
- The vehicle, crew and total cost calculations.
- The contamination results and the falling number of missed collections.

## Recommended changes
1. Replace the claim that participation was "broadly similar" with the actual gap, and propose a tailored approach for flats.
2. Re-project tonnage by housing type using the pilot rates (about 2,870 tonnes), and add a downside case.
3. Address the Brookfield capacity limit: cost the second plant, including gate fee and haulage, or find an alternative.
4. Add the missing cost lines and set out the capital funding position.
5. Restate the funding conclusion. On corrected figures, the service needs funding beyond the £520,000 provisional allocation.
6. Update the cover note. Its claims that participation held up in flats, that treatment is local, that every cost line is shown, and that the service is fully funded are all not supported as written.
